text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thank you for contacting me, C. I'm sorry about your father's death.

I want to help the three of you find a plan that works for everyone. I'm not able to make legal decisions or move money, but I can help you talk things through and keep track of what each of you needs.

To start, could you tell me what matters most to you? For example, do you want the house sold or kept, and what worries you about A's offer? Also, do you know what the will says about the house, and whether anyone has read it since the death?

I'll also write to A and B and ask for their concerns. Once I hear from everyone, I'll put together a list of concerns and share it with all of you so you can check it and correct me.

I’m open to selling or keeping the house, but I want a fair financial share. I haven’t agreed to A buying it at a discount, and I won’t subsidize that. I don’t know what the will says or whether anyone has read it. There’s no rush from me.

I'm helping your family sort out what happens with your father's house, at C's request. I'm sorry about your father's death.

I'm writing to B as well, and I'll share a list of everyone's concerns with all three of you so you can check it.

Thank you. I’m not sure yet what should happen to the house, but I’d be grateful if the estate could provide some money for me to start a dance studio. I don’t know what the will says, and I’m not sure what would be fair until we know what it provides and hear everyone’s views. I understand A wants to buy the house, and C hasn’t agreed.

Here is my first draft of the list of concerns, based on what the three of you have told me. Please tell me where it is wrong or incomplete.

1. You want a fair financial share, are open to selling or keeping the house, and will not agree to a discount purchase that leaves you subsidizing it.
2. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount, has no price in mind, and says she wants the result to be fair to you and B.
3. B has not decided about the house and would like the estate to give her money to start a dance studio.
4. None of you knows what the will says. This blocks every other item on the list.
5. My own concern: no one has told me who the executor is, or who currently has authority over the house and the estate.
6. My own concern: "fair" and "family discount" have no numbers attached, so I cannot weigh any plan against this list until we have a shared figure for what the house is worth.
7. My own concern: you have said there is no rush, but A and B have not said how much time they need.

Two questions for you. Do you know who the executor is, and can you get a copy of the will? I cannot read it for you or advise you legally, but the three of you need the same information in front of you.

Please disagree with me freely. I keep the list, so tell me what I have got wrong.

I don’t know who the executor is, and I can’t get the will yet. Item 4 should say I don’t know what it says or whether it’s been read; I can’t speak for A and B. The rest looks right from my perspective.

Here is the part I want to say plainly, and you may disagree with it. A discount is not separate from the shares. If A pays less than the house is worth, the difference comes out of B's and C's pockets unless it is counted against A's own share of the estate. So the fair version of A's plan is one where the discount is treated as part of what A receives, and B and C are made whole for it. The same goes for B's dance studio money: it has to come from somewhere in the estate, and the will tells us where.

Do you agree with that way of framing it?

Broadly, yes: any discount should be counted, not quietly taken from my share. But we don’t yet know what the will or legal rules require, so I wouldn’t say the will alone settles where B’s money comes from.
